t: Beowulf survives only in the Nowell Codex, copied between about 975 and 1025; when the poem was composed, and whether it was passed down orally first, is still debated.
It tells of a Geatish hero who frees the Danish king Hrothgar's hall from Grendel and his mother and dies, fifty years later, fighting a dragon.
Damaged in the Ashburnham House fire of 1731, the manuscript was first transcribed in 1786, and the poem has since been translated hundreds of times.
dyk: The manuscript's shelfmark, Cotton Vitellius A.XV, means the 15th book from the left on the top shelf of the bookcase in Robert Cotton's library that had a bust of the Roman emperor Vitellius on top.
ev: King Hygelac's raid into Frisia, told in the poem, is recorded by Gregory of Tours
The only surviving manuscript, the Nowell Codex, is written by two scribes
Laurence Nowell, after whom the codex is named, most likely acquires it, according to Kevin Kiernan
Fire at Ashburnham House chars the manuscript's margins and destroys some readings
Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin makes the first transcriptions of the manuscript
Frederick Klaeber publishes the edition that becomes the central source for study of the poem
J. R. R. Tolkien's lecture Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics opens modern criticism
Seamus Heaney's verse translation is published

f.made: An anonymous author known as the "Beowulf poet"; its date of composition is disputed, from the 8th century to near the date of the manuscript, which was copied by two scribes
f.form: An Old English poem of 3,182 alliterative lines, mostly in the Late West Saxon dialect with many other dialect forms
f.where: The Nowell Codex, British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.XV, London
f.known: Beowulf's fights with Grendel, Grendel's mother and the dragon; the mead hall Heorot; alliterative verse and kennings; the mix of pagan setting and Christian outlook; the fire of 1731; Tolkien's lecture of 1936
